module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 348

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/348](https://www.erdosproblems.com/348)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos348

open Erdos348

/--
For what values of $0 \leq m < n$ is there a complete sequence
$A = \{a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots\}$ of integers such that
 1. $A$ remains complete after removing any $m$ elements, but
 2. $A$ is not complete after removing any $n$ elements.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_348 :
    { (m, n) | (m) (n) (_ : m < n) (a : ℕ → ℕ) (_ : Monotone a)
      (_ : ∀ s, s.card = m → IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (Function.updateFinset a s 0))
        (_ : ∀ t, t.card = n → ¬IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (Function.updateFinset a t 0)) } =
    answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

end Erdos348

reformulations.difference: The source deletes m (resp. n) terms from a complete sequence of positive integers a_1 <= a_2 <= ... . The Lean instead zeroes the entries indexed by a Finset `s` (`Function.updateFinset a s 0`) of a monotone `a : ℕ → ℕ` that may itself contain zero terms. It also does not separately require that `a` be complete.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (i) A zero entry adds nothing to any finite index-subset sum, so the subset sums of `updateFinset a s 0` are exactly those of the sequence with the indices in s deleted. I proved `∑ i ∈ B, updateFinset a t 0 i = ∑ i ∈ B.filter (· ∉ t), a i` in Lean. (ii) Deleting terms only shrinks the subset-sum set, and some s of card m always exists. So condition 1 already forces `a` to be complete, and the source's 'complete sequence' clause is implied. (iii) Zeros cannot create new pairs. A monotone `a` is either identically 0 (not complete) or has k < ∞ leading zeros followed by a positive monotone tail b. Condition 1 for `a` is equivalent to: every m-deletion from b keeps completeness. Condition 2 for `a` is equivalent to: every max(0, n−k)-deletion from b destroys completeness. So n−k > m, since otherwise conditions 1 and 2 contradict each other. Then every n-deletion from b also destroys completeness, because every n-set contains an (n−k)-set and non-completeness persists under further deletion. Hence b witnesses (m,n) in the source's sense. Conversely, every positive witness is a Lean witness. The Lean set therefore equals the source's set of pairs. Separately, requiring monotonicity loses nothing: a multiset with some value of infinite multiplicity can never satisfy condition 2, since deleting copies of that value never changes the subset sums.

review.notes:
No misformalization found. The file has a single declaration, Erdos348.erdos_348.

Reading of condition 2. The source's ambiguous "A is not complete after removing any n elements" is formalized with a universal quantifier: every n-deletion destroys completeness. This is the source's intended reading.
- van Doorn's note paraphrases the problem as "N \ P(A \ S) is finite for any set S with |S| = m, whereas N \ P(A \ S) is infinite for any set S with |S| = n".
- The site says the case (2,3) is not known. Under the existential reading, the multiset in the forum discussion (1,1,1,2,2,3,3,5,8,8,13,...) would already settle it: it survives every 2-deletion and breaks after deleting {8,8,13}. The poster notes it is "not a witness" because scattered triples heal.
- The proof claim on the site uses the same universal reading.

Notion of completeness. `IsAddCompleteNatSeq'` is the weak notion: all sufficiently large integers are sums over distinct indices. This matches the site's convention (#346, #349) and its remark that "Erdős and Graham most likely meant the weaker notion". The forum records that the formalization was updated to this notion in September 2025.

Sanity checks.
- `#print` confirms the set-builder elaborates to {x : ℕ × ℕ | ∃ m n (_ : m < n) a (_ : Monotone a) (_ : ∀ s : Finset ℕ, s.card = m → ...) (_ : ∀ t : Finset ℕ, t.card = n → ¬...), (m, n) = x}.
- I proved in Lean that (0,1) is in the set, with a i = 2^i, as the source says.
- A Perl computation on the Fibonacci multiset 1,1,2,3,5,... supports (1,2) under the Lean semantics. With terms F_1..F_21, every single deletion leaves all numbers up to 17,710 representable. With terms F_1..F_22, every pair deletion tested (120 pairs, avoiding the truncation edge) leaves a whole parity class of the top values F_k − 1 unrepresentable, i.e. infinitely many exceptions.

Status. `research open` matches erdosproblems.com (OPEN) and the teorth database. There is one unverified full proof claim by Jesse Geneson (AI-assisted, submitted 2026-09-09, ResearchGate preprint 'Deletion thresholds for complete sequences'). It claims that only m ∈ {0,1} work. If accepted, the answer would be {(m,n) | m < n ∧ m ≤ 1}. It has not been accepted, so I report no status issue.

Original wording. The Erdős–Graham 1980 PDF (math.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf) is a scan with no text layer and no OCR tool was available, so I could not check the original wording directly. I relied on the site's LaTeX and van Doorn's paraphrase, which agree with each other.

Outside this file. The docstring of `IsAddCompleteNatSeq'` in FormalConjecturesForMathlib says "(not necessarily distinct) terms". The definition correctly sums over distinct indices, allowing repeated values, which is the intended multiset semantics.
